Chapter Two: Habits That Form the Heart—How Everyday Practices Shape Desire.
Let’s dive in. Most of us don’t realize just how powerful our habits really are. It’s tempting to see routines as boring or even a little mindless, isn’t it? But here’s the thing—those little everyday actions? They’re actually the training ground for what we care about most.
Think about your own mornings for a second. The way you start your day, those automatic moves before you’re even fully awake—they’re quietly shaping your heart. Picture a teenager waking up and, almost on autopilot, grabbing her phone to scroll through social media. At first, it’s just about catching up with friends. But before long, that habit becomes as natural as breathing. The phone’s the first thing she reaches for, even before her feet hit the floor.
What she might not notice is how this simple routine is reshaping her desires. She starts to crave attention, to measure her worth by likes and comments. That little habit teaches her what matters, turning a morning ritual into a daily lesson about value and identity.
Now, let’s peek into a different household. Here, every evening, a family circles around the dinner table. They light a candle, say a quiet prayer, and swap stories from their day. Doesn’t sound flashy, does it? But over time, this small ritual leaves a big impression. The kids learn that dinner’s about more than just eating—it’s about connection, gratitude, and belonging. The habit shapes their hearts, gently teaching them what to love.
Most of the time, we don’t pick our habits on purpose. We just absorb them from the world around us, sometimes without even realizing it. Our culture is packed with what you might call “secular liturgies”—these are practices that shape our desires in subtle but powerful ways.
Take a trip to the mall, for example. On the surface, it’s just shopping. But think about the music, the displays, the constant promise of something new. It’s all designed to stir up longing, to make you want more. The mall becomes almost like a temple, shaping what we love and teaching us to crave consumption.
And it doesn’t stop there. These everyday rituals—the rhythm of your workweek, the way you unwind with entertainment, even how you greet a friend—carry messages about what’s important. Over time, they sink into your bones, shaping your heart’s deepest loves.
It’s so easy to overlook how deeply these habits form us. We tell ourselves that as long as we believe the right things, our lives will naturally follow. But here’s something to pay attention to—the heart is shaped by what it does, not just by what it thinks. The things you repeat, day after day, become the grooves along which your desires run.
That’s why spiritual formation isn’t just about ideas. It’s about practices—habits that aim your heart toward what’s truly good. In the Christian tradition, worship is more than just expressing belief; it’s a way of training desire, forming your heart to love God and neighbor.
But here’s the catch—this kind of formation doesn’t happen by accident. It takes intention. It means paying attention to the habits that are shaping your life and choosing practices that point your heart in a better direction. Sure, it’s a slow journey, full of small steps and quiet routines. But over time, these habits become the foundation for a life that’s truly well-lived.
